summary: The Omoda 9 SHS is Chery's flagship in Australia and is sold here in a single $61,990 Virtue AWD grade, pairing a 1.5-litre turbo petrol with three electric motors for 395kW, a 4.9-second 0-100km/h claim and 145km of WLTP electric range from a 34.46kWh battery — roughly double the electric range of a BYD Sealion 6 or Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV for similar money. Australian reviewers are consistent that the powertrain, equipment list and cabin quality are the strongest part of the car and that the chassis is not: CarExpert, CarsGuide, Chasing Cars and carsales all criticise vague steering, loose body control and a busy, head-tossing ride, and none rates it as a genuine premium drive. It is a compelling equipment-and-range package with a hard ceiling on driving polish, and with no resale history in a brand that launched here in 2025.
pros: 145km of WLTP electric-only range from a 34.46kWh usable battery — around double a BYD Sealion 6 Premium AWD (81km) or a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV, and enough that most Melbourne buyers would rarely start the engine
395kW/650Nm from a 1.5-litre turbo petrol and three motors gives a claimed 4.9-second 0-100km/h, quicker than any PHEV SUV near the price and quicker than most $100k performance SUVs
70kW DC fast charging (30-80 per cent in about 25 minutes) plus 6.6kW AC — the Sealion 6 and Outlander PHEV have no DC capability at all, so an Omoda 9 can top up its electric range on a road trip

Eight-year/unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty with a matching eight-year/unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty guaranteeing at least 70 per cent residual capacity, plus eight years of capped-price servicing ($3343 total) and roadside assistance

1500kg braked towing and a 660-litre boot (1783 litres folded) — the Jaecoo J7 SHS has no braked tow rating at all and only 340 litres, and the seven-seat Chery Tiggo 8 PHEV leaves just 117 litres behind its third row
cons: Omoda's own figure for a depleted battery is 7.0L/100km, not the 1.4L/100km combined label, and a 2000km European test returned 7.2L/100km — a 2.2-tonne AWD SUV on 95-octane premium, so the running-cost case collapses for anyone who cannot charge at home

Ride and steering are the near-universal complaint: CarExpert calls it a 'bouncy, head-tossing ride', CarsGuide marks it down for 'vague steering' and 'lacking body control', and Chasing Cars describes the steering as 'numb and lifeless' — it does not drive like the premium car its price and equipment imply
Five seats only, where a Chery Tiggo 8 Super Hybrid at $42,990 and several rivals at this money seat seven, and the front seats lack height and tilt adjustment despite being power-operated

Omoda launched in Australia in 2025 with one model and a small dealer network, and the flagship is already being advertised with a $5000 factory bonus — resale is unproven and the transaction price keeps resetting, which is why a steeper-than-average depreciation curve is assumed here
Only one grade is offered, so there is no cheaper way into the nameplate: the choice is $61,990 or nothing, roughly $20,000 above the closely related Jaecoo J7 SHS Track
